## Introduction

How well does a network keep functioning as its nodes disappear? Albert,
Jeong & Barabasi (2000) <doi:10.1038/35019019> showed that many real
networks respond very differently to two kinds of node loss: **random
failure**, where nodes disappear independently of any property of the
network, and **targeted attack**, where the most "important" nodes (by
degree, betweenness, or another centrality) are removed first. Some
networks barely notice random failure but collapse quickly under a
targeted attack on their hubs.

netRobust simulates both scenarios on any `igraph` object -- directed or
undirected, weighted or not -- tracks a set of robustness indicators
(giant component size, mean distance, connectivity, and others) as
nodes are removed, and provides a Monte Carlo framework for asking
whether an observed curve is *statistically* more damaging than chance
alone would produce. This vignette walks through that full workflow, end
to end, on a network with a documented real-world outcome to check the
results against: does the network actually single out the two people who
turned out, historically, to matter most?

## Quick reference: which question does which function answer?

| Question | Function(s) |
|---|---|
| How does my network degrade under random failure vs. a targeted attack? | `random_failures()`, `attack_by_*()`, `robustness()`, `plot_robustness()` |
| Is the attack significantly worse than random failure -- overall? | `robustness_null_removal()`, `compare_robustness_index_to_null()`, `plot_r_index_null()` |
| At which removal step does that difference actually show up? | `compare_to_null()` |
| Same questions, but for losing relationships (edges) instead of actors (nodes)? | `random_edge_failures()`, `attack_by_edge_*()`, `edge_robustness()`, `edge_robustness_null_removal()` |
| Is removing this one node -- or this specific group -- unusually damaging? | `knockout_robustness()`, `knockout_robustness_null_removal()`, `compare_knockout_to_null()`, `plot_knockout_null()` |
| Which node matters most, fairly, averaged across every possible removal order? | `shapley_robustness()`, `plot_shapley()` |
| Is my network's structure itself unusually vulnerable, compared to other networks its size? | `robustness_null_structural()` |

## Setup

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(netRobust)
library(igraph)
```

One dependency is optional and only changes *how* the Monte Carlo
simulations run, never their results:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
future::plan(future::multisession)   # parallelise replicates across cores
```

Sequential replicates already show a console progress indicator (a
spinner and percentage) with no setup needed -- it's skipped when
running in parallel, since a `future.apply` worker has no access to the
parent session's console.

## Example network: Zachary's Karate Club

netRobust ships Zachary's Karate Club as built-in data: 34 members of a
university karate club and the 78 friendships between them, recorded by
Wayne W. Zachary (1977) before the club split into two rival factions.
Unlike the bare edge list many packages ship, this copy (`?karate`) keeps
Zachary's original **edge weights** (interaction strength, `1`-`7`) and
each member's **`Faction`** -- which of the two groups they actually
joined once the club split. That split is the real-world outcome the
robustness/knock-out/Shapley results below get checked against.

```{r}
data(karate)
g <- karate
g
table(V(g)$Faction)
```

```{r}
plot(g, vertex.label = NA, vertex.size = 8,
     vertex.color = c("steelblue", "tomato")[V(g)$Faction],
     edge.width = E(g)$weight / 3, edge.color = "grey70",
     main = "Zachary's Karate Club (colour = eventual faction, width = tie strength)")
```

It's undirected but genuinely weighted, which lets the rest of this
vignette demonstrate `weights_as=` on real data instead of a synthetic
example. Section
["A note on direction and weights"](#a-note-on-direction-and-weights)
covers both.

## Removal orders

Every scenario in netRobust starts from a **removal order**: which
vertex goes first, second, and so on. `random_failures()` generates a
uniformly random order; `attack_by_degree()` removes the highest-degree
("hub") vertices first, the classic attack criterion from Albert et al.
(2000).

```{r}
set.seed(1)
r <- random_failures(g)
d <- attack_by_degree(g)
head(d)
```

John A (the club president, degree 17) and Mr Hi (the instructor, degree
16) are removed first -- unsurprising, since the whole club revolved
around these two long before it split around them. Both return the same
shape: a named integer vector, first element = first vertex removed.
Five more targeted-attack criteria exist -- `attack_by_betweenness()`,
`attack_by_closeness()`, `attack_by_eigenvector()`, `attack_by_pagerank()`,
and `attack_by_hits()` (Kleinberg's hub or authority scores, for directed
networks) -- with the same `function(g) -> removal order` contract.

## A note on direction and weights

On a directed graph, "degree" is ambiguous: a vertex can have many
incoming connections and few outgoing ones, or vice versa.
`attack_by_degree()` and `attack_by_closeness()` expose
`mode = c("all", "out", "in")` (ignored on undirected graphs, like the
Karate Club above) to control which one drives the attack; the other
attacks follow edge direction as their own measure defines it (e.g.
hub vs. authority in `attack_by_hits()`). To see why this matters, take
a tiny directed toy graph with one "out-hub" and one "in-hub":

```{r}
toy <- graph_from_literal(A -+ B, A -+ C, A -+ D, B -+ D, C -+ D, E -+ D)
```

```{r}
plot(toy, edge.arrow.size = 0.6, vertex.color = "steelblue",
     main = "A has the highest out-degree, D the highest in-degree")
```

```{r}
attack_by_degree(toy, mode = "out")   # A goes first: highest out-degree
attack_by_degree(toy, mode = "in")    # D goes first: highest in-degree
```

Same graph, same criterion (degree), opposite first casualty -- purely
because of which direction "degree" was counted in. `robustness()` and
the `attack_by_*()` functions default to `directed = NULL`, which
auto-detects from `is_directed(g)`; pass `directed =` explicitly only to
override that.

The betweenness/closeness/eigenvector/PageRank attacks take a parallel
`weights_as = c("distance", "strength")` argument for *weighted*
networks, telling netRobust how to interpret an edge weight: as a
**distance** (bigger weight = farther apart, used as-is) or as a
**strength** (bigger weight = closer/stronger tie, inverted before
being used as a distance). The Karate Club's weights are interaction
strengths, so this actually matters here:

```{r}
b_strength <- attack_by_betweenness(g, weights_as = "strength")
b_distance <- attack_by_betweenness(g, weights_as = "distance")
head(names(b_strength), 4)
head(names(b_distance), 4)
```

Both remove Mr Hi first, but diverge immediately after: treating the
weights as *strengths* removes Actor 3 second, while treating the exact
same numbers as *distances* removes John A second instead -- the same
weight column, read two different ways, produces two different attack
orders. Get this backwards on your own weighted network and every
downstream result below would answer a question you didn't mean to ask.

# Part 1: Is my network vulnerable to failure or attack, overall?

## Robustness curves

`robustness()` takes a removal order and returns one row per removal
step, with one column per indicator. `keep =` picks a subset of the
built-in indicators (see `?robustness` for the full default set, and how
to add your own via `indicators =`):

```{r}
failure <- robustness(g, ids = r, keep = c("giant_component_size", "mean_distance", "connectivity"))
attack  <- robustness(g, ids = d, keep = c("giant_component_size", "mean_distance", "connectivity"))
head(attack)
```

`giant_component_size` already tells a story: removing hub nodes
by degree shrinks it far faster than removing the same number of random
nodes. But `failure` here is a single random draw -- one arbitrary
sample out of the enormous space of possible removal orders. The next
section builds the full distribution instead of relying on one sample.

## Building a null model

`robustness_null_removal()` repeats `random_failures()` +
`robustness()` many times on the *same* network, producing the
empirical distribution of every indicator at every removal step --
i.e., what random failure alone typically looks like, and how much it
varies. `summarise_null()` collapses that into a mean/median and a 95%
quantile envelope, ready for plotting.

```{r}
null_dist <- robustness_null_removal(g, n_reps = 200, seed = 123,
                                      keep = c("giant_component_size", "mean_distance", "connectivity"))
null_env  <- summarise_null(null_dist)
head(null_env)
```

The `...` in `robustness_null_removal(g, ..., keep = c(...))` must match
whatever settings were used for the observed curve it will be compared
against (here, `attack`) -- same indicators, same `directed =`/weights
treatment -- for the comparison to be valid.

## Plotting

A single random draw isn't a meaningful stand-in for "the failure
scenario" once hundreds of replicates of it already exist. So instead of
plotting one arbitrary `failure` curve, we plot the null distribution's
**median** curve instead -- leave `failure=` out and `plot_robustness()`
derives it from `null_envelope` itself (`summary = "median"` is the
default; pass `summary = "mean"` for the mean curve instead):

```{r, warning = FALSE}
fig <- plot_robustness(attack = attack, null_envelope = null_env)
fig
```

`plot_robustness()` labels that derived curve "Failures (median)" and
adds a caption explaining the shaded band automatically -- guaranteed to
match what was actually plotted, since the function performed the
derivation itself rather than trusting a hand-pivoted curve to really be
the median (see `?plot_robustness` if you'd rather supply your own
`failure=` curve, e.g. a single random draw, alongside the null
envelope). The attack curve drops well below the failure envelope almost
immediately: losing the two highest-degree members fragments the club
far faster than losing any two members at random would.

## Does the attack differ from random failure overall?

Two complementary questions can be asked of an attack curve: *does it
differ from random failure at all*, taking the whole curve together, and
*at which removal step* does that difference show up. This section
answers the first (the global question); the next section answers the
second (the pointwise one).

`robustness_index()` collapses a whole curve to one number -- the R-index
of Schneider et al. (2011) <doi:10.1073/pnas.1009440108>, generalised
here to any indicator (see `?robustness_index` for the formula). It's
deliberately neutral about whether a higher or lower value is
"good": for `giant_component_size` specifically it's bounded in `[0, 1]` (1 = the curve
never moved from its intact-network value), but that bound and its
reading don't carry over to every indicator -- `diameter`/`mean_distance`, for
example, typically *increase* under attack before a network fragments,
so their R-index can exceed 1 without anything having "improved".

`compare_robustness_index_to_null()` compares one observed R-index
against the null's own distribution of R-index values (one per
replicate) and returns an empirical p-value -- a single verdict for the
whole curve, with none of the multiple-comparisons issue that testing
every removal step separately would carry:

```{r}
compare_robustness_index_to_null(attack, null_dist, index = "giant_component_size")
```

The degree attack's R-index (`0.17`) sits far below the null's mean
(`0.44`) -- on average across the whole removal sequence, the giant
component is barely a sixth of its intact size under this attack, versus
staying near half its size under random loss -- and the empirical
p-value is `0`, i.e. none of the 200 random-failure replicates came
anywhere close. The same comparison, visually -- a histogram of the
null's R-index values, with the attack's own R-index marked as a dashed
line:

```{r, fig.height = 4}
plot_r_index_null(null_dist, observed = attack, index = "giant_component_size")
```

`compare_robustness()` applies `robustness_index()` across several
deterministic attack curves at once, for a descriptive (not yet
statistical) side-by-side comparison; `robustness_index_null()` is its
counterpart for a null distribution's many replicates (averaging the
R-index *per replicate*, not the R-index of an already-averaged curve --
see `?robustness_index_null` for why that distinction matters):

```{r}
b <- attack_by_betweenness(g)
c <- attack_by_closeness(g)
e <- attack_by_eigenvector(g)
p <- attack_by_pagerank(g)

attack_b <- robustness(g, ids = b, keep = c("giant_component_size", "mean_distance", "connectivity"))
attack_c <- robustness(g, ids = c, keep = c("giant_component_size", "mean_distance", "connectivity"))
attack_e <- robustness(g, ids = e, keep = c("giant_component_size", "mean_distance", "connectivity"))
attack_p <- robustness(g, ids = p, keep = c("giant_component_size", "mean_distance", "connectivity"))

r_index_attacks <- compare_robustness(scenario_list = list(
  Degree = attack, Betweenness = attack_b, Closeness = attack_c,
  Eigenvector = attack_e, PageRank = attack_p
), index = "giant_component_size")

r_index_failures <- data.frame(Scenario = "Failures", Index = "giant_component_size",
                                R_index = robustness_index_null(null_dist, index = "giant_component_size"))

rbind(r_index_failures, r_index_attacks)
```

Every targeted attack scores well below random failure on this network
-- the Karate Club, like most real networks with a handful of highly
connected hubs, is far more vulnerable to targeted attacks than to
random ones.

## Where along the curve does the difference show up?

`compare_to_null()` answers the pointwise question: at *which* removal
step does the attack become significantly worse than random failure,
per indicator. It complements the R-index comparison above rather than
repeating it -- one gives a single overall verdict, this one localises
*where* along the curve a difference happens, at the cost of not
correcting for testing many steps independently (`?compare_to_null` has
the detail):

```{r}
sig <- compare_to_null(attack, null_dist)
gc_sig <- sig[sig$Index == "giant_component_size", ]
head(gc_sig, 6)
```

Removing just John A and Mr Hi (`N = 1`-`2`) isn't yet distinguishable
from random loss (`p = 1`) -- the club tolerates losing any two members,
even these two, without visibly more damage than chance. The picture
flips fast: by the third removal `p` drops to `0.05`, and from the
fourth removal on `p = 0`. Three or four members in, the *identity* of
who's missing starts to matter far more than random loss ever would.

## Removing edges instead of nodes

Everything so far has removed *nodes* -- actors disappearing entirely.
Sometimes the question is narrower: what happens if specific
*relationships* are lost, without the actors themselves leaving the
network? `random_edge_failures()` and `attack_by_edge_betweenness()`/
`attack_by_edge_weight()` are the edge-level counterparts of
`random_failures()`/`attack_by_*()`; `edge_robustness()` is the
edge-level counterpart of `robustness()`:

```{r}
er <- random_edge_failures(g)
ea <- attack_by_edge_betweenness(g)

efailure <- edge_robustness(g, ids = er, keep = c("giant_component_size", "connectivity"))
eattack  <- edge_robustness(g, ids = ea, keep = c("giant_component_size", "connectivity"))
head(eattack)
```

`edge_robustness()` produces the exact same shape as `robustness()` (`N` +
one column per indicator), so it plugs directly into every function
already introduced -- with **no changes needed** -- as long as the null
distribution it's compared against was itself built from
`random_edge_failures()` replicates, not node-removal ones.
`edge_robustness_null_removal()` is the edge-level counterpart of
`robustness_null_removal()` for exactly that:

```{r}
edge_null <- edge_robustness_null_removal(g, n_reps = 200, seed = 123,
                                           keep = c("giant_component_size", "connectivity"))
compare_robustness_index_to_null(eattack, edge_null, index = "giant_component_size")
```

```{r, fig.height = 4}
plot_r_index_null(edge_null, observed = eattack, index = "giant_component_size")
```

Same reading as the node-level version: removing the edges that carry
the most betweenness is significantly more damaging than losing the same
number of random relationships. Now that real weights are available,
`attack_by_edge_weight()` can rank edges directly by tie strength --
worth asking whether removing the *strongest* ties first is actually the
most damaging edge strategy, or whether something else is:

```{r}
ew_strong <- attack_by_edge_weight(g, weights_as = "strength")               # strongest ties first
ew_weak   <- attack_by_edge_weight(g, weights_as = "strength", decreasing = FALSE)  # weakest first

eattack_strong <- edge_robustness(g, ids = ew_strong, keep = c("giant_component_size"))
eattack_weak   <- edge_robustness(g, ids = ew_weak,   keep = c("giant_component_size"))

compare_robustness(scenario_list = list(
  Betweenness = eattack, `Weight (strongest first)` = eattack_strong,
  `Weight (weakest first)` = eattack_weak
), index = "giant_component_size")
```

Neither R-index alone says whether that gap from random edge loss is
real or just noise -- the same null distribution built above answers
that for both:

```{r}
compare_robustness_index_to_null(eattack_strong, edge_null, index = "giant_component_size")
compare_robustness_index_to_null(eattack_weak, edge_null, index = "giant_component_size")
```

A genuine surprise: removing the *strongest* ties first is barely
different from random edge loss and, per the first test above, not
significant. Removing the *weakest* ties first, despite scoring worse
(a lower, more damaging R-index) than betweenness alone, comes out
significantly *more* damaging than random edge loss in the second test.
Strong ties here mostly reinforce connections that already exist through
other paths; weak ties are more often the only link between two
otherwise-separate parts of the club -- an edge-level echo of
Granovetter's "strength of weak ties." If your weights represent
a *cost/distance* instead (lower = stronger tie) rather than a
*strength*, pass `weights_as = "distance"` so `decreasing = TRUE` still
means "strongest tie first" -- see `?attack_by_edge_weight`.

**A structural fact worth knowing:** under edge removal, `edge_density` is
*mathematically identical* across every scenario on the same graph, not
just similar -- it depends only on how many edges have been removed, never
on which ones (the vertex count never changes). See
`?edge_robustness`'s "edge_density is order-invariant here" section before
reading anything into an `edge_density` comparison here.

**Parallel edges** (multiple edges between the same pair of vertices)
would break the internal by-edge identification these functions rely on;
by default they're collapsed automatically (summing weights, with a
warning) via `on_parallel = "collapse"` -- pass `"error"` instead if
you'd rather that stop and let you resolve it yourself.

# Part 2: Which specific nodes matter?

## Testing nodes in isolation (knock-out)

A different question from Part 1: not "how does the network degrade as
removal accumulates?" but "what's the effect of *this* node -- or this
specific *set* of nodes -- disappearing, on its own, independent of any
other removal?" `knockout_robustness()` answers that: every group is
tested against the *intact* network and then discarded, never against
the result of a previous group's removal.

```{r}
ko <- knockout_robustness(g, keep = c("giant_component_size"))
head(ko)
```

With no `groups=` argument, every vertex is tested individually -- one
row per node, plus a first reference row (`group_id = 0`) for the intact
network itself (`include_intact = TRUE` is the default), so every group's
effect sits in the same table as the baseline it's implicitly compared
against. That's enough to answer "which single node's loss does the most
damage?" -- the reference row is never picked up here, since the intact
network is never the most damaging outcome:

```{r}
ko[which.min(ko$giant_component_size), ]
```

Mr Hi, alone, shrinks the giant component from 34 to 27 members -- more
than any other single member. `groups=` accepts an explicit list
instead, for specific combinations you care about -- each element either
vertex names or vertex indices:

```{r}
knockout_robustness(g, groups = list(c("Mr Hi", "John A")), keep = c("giant_component_size"))
```

Removing both club leaders together shrinks the giant component further
still, to 26. The `group` column is a list-column holding the exact
(deduplicated) set of vertices removed in that trial; `n_removed` is its
size. Unlike `robustness()`/`edge_robustness()`, there's no
`N`/sequential-step column here at all -- each row is an independent
trial, not a point on a trajectory.

### Is a particular group's effect unusual?

`compare_to_null()`/`robustness_index()` assume a *trajectory* (an `N`
column) -- they don't apply here directly. The natural question for a
knock-out is different anyway: not "does this differ from random failure
overall?" but *"is removing this particular node -- or this particular
group -- more damaging than removing a random one of the same size?"*
That's a null stratified by group size, since a 1-vertex and a 2-vertex
knock-out aren't on the same scale to begin with:

```{r}
knull <- knockout_robustness_null_removal(g, sizes = c(1, 2), n_reps = 200, seed = 123,
                                           keep = c("giant_component_size"))
```

Compare Mr Hi alone, and the two leaders together, against same-size
random groups:

```{r}
worst <- ko[which.min(ko$giant_component_size), ]
pair  <- knockout_robustness(g, groups = list(c("Mr Hi", "John A")), keep = c("giant_component_size"),
                              include_intact = FALSE)

observed <- rbind(worst, pair)
observed$group_id <- seq_len(nrow(observed))

compare_knockout_to_null(observed, knull, index = "giant_component_size")
```

Both come out significant: Mr Hi is unusually damaging alone, and the
two leaders stay unusually damaging together. Visually, one panel per
group size, each observed group as its own coloured line:

```{r, fig.height = 4}
plot_knockout_null(knull, observed = observed, index = "giant_component_size")
```

An observed group whose size wasn't included in `sizes=` when building
the null errors in `compare_knockout_to_null()` (the p-value would be
undefined) but only warns in `plot_knockout_null()` (it's a visual aid,
not a significance test -- the line still draws, just without a
histogram behind it).

## Node importance via Shapley values

Knock-out asks about *one* node, or one specific group, in isolation.
A different question: *averaged over every possible removal order, how
much does each node matter?* That's a Shapley value (Shapley 1953) --
a node's fair share of the total change in an indicator, credited for
its impact across every context it could be removed in (early, late,
alongside any combination of other removed nodes), not just the one
order a single attack curve happens to trace out.

It's computed efficiently: a single random removal order already gives
every node's marginal contribution for free (the change in an indicator
between consecutive steps), so `n_reps` random orders -- the same
simulation `random_failures()` + `robustness()` already run -- estimate
every node's Shapley value simultaneously, in one pass per replicate:

```{r}
shap <- shapley_robustness(g, n_reps = 200, n_perm = 200, seed = 123,
                            keep = c("giant_component_size", "mean_distance"))
head(shap$nodes[order(-shap$nodes$giant_component_size), ])
```

`shap$nodes` is one row per vertex, with a value and a standard-error
column per indicator. The values satisfy Shapley's *efficiency* axiom:
they sum exactly to the indicator's intact-network value minus its
value once every node is gone (`vcount(g)` minus `0`, for
`giant_component_size`):

```{r}
sum(shap$nodes$giant_component_size)
```

### Is there real signal, or just noise?

Comparing every node against every other one directly would take
`choose(vcount(g), 2)` pairwise tests -- impractical for anything but a
tiny network, and it reintroduces the same multiple-comparisons problem
that `compare_robustness_index_to_null()` avoids by testing a whole curve
at once instead of step by step. `shapley_robustness()` sidesteps this
with a single **global** test per indicator instead: are nodes more
differentiated from each other than sampling noise alone would produce?

```{r}
shap$global_test
```

Both indicators come back significant (`p = 0`): nodes genuinely differ
in importance here, not just by chance. That answers *whether* nodes
differ at all -- not *which* nodes differ from which. For that, the
per-node standard errors already in `shap$nodes` support an informal
visual comparison instead, via `plot_shapley()` (a forest plot, one
panel per indicator, node order fixed across panels so a node's
position can be tracked between them):

```{r, fig.height = 6}
plot_shapley(shap)
```

Mr Hi and John A are, by a wide margin, the two most important nodes on
both indicators -- their confidence intervals don't overlap with any
other member's. That's exactly where this vignette's opening question
gets answered: `V(g)$Faction` records which of the two factions each
member actually joined once the club split in 1977, and Mr Hi and John A
ended up on **opposite** factions (`1` and `2`).

```{r}
data.frame(node = c("Mr Hi", "John A"), Faction = V(g)$Faction[c(1, 34)])
```

The two nodes the Shapley values single out as most important, with no
knowledge of the split whatsoever, are exactly the two people the club's
real fission ended up centring on.

# Part 3: Is my network's structure itself unusual?

## Structural null model

`robustness_null_removal()` (Part 1) asks: *given this exact network,
does this attack strategy do more damage than chance?* A different
question is: *is this network's structure itself unusually vulnerable to
this attack strategy, compared to other networks the same size with the
same degree sequence?* `robustness_null_structural()` answers that one
instead, by rewiring the network (preserving each vertex's degree)
rather than randomising the removal order:

```{r}
struct_null <- robustness_null_structural(g, attack_fn = attack_by_degree,
                                           n_reps = 200, seed = 123,
                                           keep = c("giant_component_size", "mean_distance", "connectivity"))
compare_robustness_index_to_null(attack, struct_null, index = "giant_component_size")
```

The degree attack's observed R-index (`0.17`) sits below the structural
null's mean (`0.22`) with `p = 0.005`: this specific arrangement of ties
-- not just the fact that a couple of members happen to have high degree
-- makes the club more vulnerable to a degree-based attack than the
typical network with the same size and degree sequence would be. This is
a **pure topological** null model: edge weights, if any, are dropped
before rewiring, since there's no principled way to carry them over onto
a randomised topology. Pass a weight-agnostic `attack_fn` (like
`attack_by_degree` above) when using it.

## Where to go next

Every function used here has a `?` help page with the full set of
arguments and further detail -- start with `?karate` for the example
network's own documentation, then `?robustness`, `?edge_robustness`,
`?knockout_robustness`, `?shapley_robustness`,
`?robustness_null_removal`, `?edge_robustness_null_removal`,
`?knockout_robustness_null_removal`, `?robustness_null_structural`, and
`?compare_robustness_index_to_null` -- or browse everything at once with
`help(package = "netRobust")`.
